In this article AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT John Ternus, chief executive officer of Apple Inc., speaks during an event in Los Angeles, California, US, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Kyle Grillot | Bloomberg | Getty Images Apple said in its annual financial filing on Tuesday that AI agents that can act in "unintended or unpredictable ways" could represent a threat to its business by opening the company up to lawsuits or hurting its reputation. The new risk factors in Apple's filing show the disruptive potential of AI agents, which have rapidly become top of mind for Silicon Valley's most important companies. "In particular, artificial intelligence agents and other technologies can take actions autonomously, including interacting with internal or external systems that in some cases they may not be authorized to access, executing or altering code, sending communications, and completing transactions," Apple wrote in the filing . The company added that agents "may behave in unintended or unpredictable ways, including by taking actions that were not directed, instructed or authorized." Earlier this year, OpenAI released Dots, and Meta introduced Muse. Both AI agents use advanced AI models to work autonomously for tasks. They can even email or remind users when new messages arrive. Apple's disclosure comes after several episodes that involved rogue AI agents breaking out of their sandboxes to hack third-party websites, like the Hugging Face incident , which has drawn renewed attention from policymakers in Washington, D.C., and around the world. Read more CNBC tech news Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents OpenAI pares fundraising goal, now seeking up to $20 billion in latest round Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion hack, says 90% of stolen user assets are covered Why AI is boosting Meta’s ad business while hurting Google search Separately, the ability of agents to use a computer in human ways is forcing big companies like Amazon and JPMorgan Chase to come up with policies around agentic access to services for strategic or security reasons. Last month, Apple announced changes to full disk access on Macs to reduce "risks related to this level of access" for AI agents installed on PCs. "The Company's ability to oversee and control third-party artificial intelligence agents and other technologies may be limited," Apple warned in its filing. Apple doesn't currently have an agentic AI. But when new CEO John Ternus was asked on Monday's earnings call about AI agents, he said that the company had "real room" to expand Siri's capabilities. "As far as agentic capabilities, we think these are promising tools for users," Ternus said. "We just want to make sure that users are aware of what they are giving access to. We want to make sure this is done in a way that protects security and privacy." watch now VIDEO 3:03 03:03 Apple looks to Siri AI to drive upgrades and offset rising costs from the AI boom Squawk on the Street This fall, Apple released Siri AI, a new assistant that uses the iPhone's local data storage to access data like calendars and emails, but Apple's Siri can't work autonomously for long stretches like Dots or Muse. Ternus said Apple can't access private data on its devices, calling it a "core differentiator." "If you think about it, so much of your personal data is on your iPhone, whether it's your contacts, your communications, health data, financial data, all of that," Ternus said. "Siri can tap into that and help you access it in a way that's very secure and private and that nobody else has access to." Commercial AI agents like those from OpenAI and Meta ask for high-level access to the user's accounts like email in order to be more useful. Apple indicated that the current regulations around AI and "super intelligence" are changing, unpredictable and that it could cost a lot of money to adapt to new laws governing AI. "In addition, the Company is subject to the risks posed by ethical concerns and negative consumer perceptions related to automation, artificial intelligence and super intelligence, including perceived threats to safety or other societal harms or complications," according to the filing. headlines.summary: The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to Bill Ackman.
headlines.article_text: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac rally on Ackman exit call Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to Bill Ackman. Both stocks have moved more than 60% higher since Oct. 14. Ackman believes both names can see a "10-fold" increase from current share prices. Bill Ackman, chief executive officer of Pershing Square Capital Management LP, center, during the company's initial public offering (IPO) on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Wednesday, April 29, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to billionaire investor Bill Ackman. Investors may agree with him, if the rally in both stocks is any sign. The Federal National Mortgage Association, known as Fannie Mae, and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, have each jumped more than 60% from Oct. 14 to Monday's close. The stocks were both up roughly 3% on Tuesday. Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, has long pushed for the two entities to be released from federal conservatorship. "The reason why it's not being touched right now is, you know, midterms," he said in an interview with CNBC's " Squawk Box ." Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae) and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation (Freddie Mac) over the last month. Ackman, who owns both names through Pershing Square, believes Freddie and Fannie have the potential to increase "10-fold from current share prices," he said in his quarterly letter to shareholders, issued on Monday. Fannie and Freddie buy mortgages from banks and other lenders, and then package them into mortgage-backed securities, known as MBS. Their operations are critical to the housing market, providing liquidity to banks and creating a secondary market for MBS. The entities were placed into conservatorship in September 2008, during the financial crisis. The stocks were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010 and have traded over the counter since then. Ackman wants the conservatorship to end, arguing the entities would be worth multiples of their current valuation if they were freed from government control. VIDEO 22:14 22:14 Watch CNBC's full interview with Bill Ackman, Pershing Square CEO President Donald Trump has supported ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie. But it remains politically and economically contentious. The entities operate under strict capital threshold requirements and would need to be recapitalized, which could happen through issuing common equity. However, the Treasury Department would need to figure out an exit plan for its roughly $388 billion ownership stake in the entities through preferred securities and warrants. Congress may also need to play a role, passing legislation to restructure the government's role in mortgage financing and home-loan guarantees. Nonetheless, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently said it could happen before Trump's term ends, telling 2Way's " The Morning Meeting " podcast that the administration will tackle the ownership structure "next year, the year after." He said affordability will be guiding the decision. One point of controversy is whether ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie would increase the spreads on MBS over Treasuries, effectively making mortgages costlier. Bessent has sought to reassure the market that wouldn't happen. "Whatever we do is going to be guided by making sure that the spread on [agency] mortgages … over the Treasury does not increase," Bessent said. Ackman argues that privatizing the GSEs would help insulate them from political meddling. "Fannie and Freddie are these massive, enormously profitable institutions where whichever political party controls them…if they're still in conservatorship, can influence the outcome of elections," he told CNBC. In one scenario, he explained, Democrats win the White House, conservatorship is still in place, and Democrats push Fannie and Freddie to lower credit standards in order to expand home ownership and affordability. "If they're going to move more aggressively into borrowers with lower credit quality, for example, to achieve a political objective, that's going to have an impact on trillions of dollars outstanding mortgage securities," Ackman said. "It's going to have an impact on overall credit spreads." MBS investors want certainty about how the entities will be run, he noted. "That only gets resolved in a world in which they exit conservatorship, they become publicly traded companies that are owned by institutional and retail investors," Ackman said. "We set the rules. headlines.article_text: CrowdStrike launches AI kill switch to control internal agents Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CrowdStrike launched an AI kill switch feature to stop and block internal agents that misbehave. The cybersecurity giant also announced a Claude Cowork integration and two AI acquisitions. Business chief Daniel Bernard told CNBC that being able to control and shut down agent activity is vital to the next wave of AI adoption. In this article CRWD Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike, speaks to the Economic Club of New York in New York City, U.S., Oct. 23, 2025. Brendan McDermid | Reuters CrowdStrike is betting that it has a solution to rogue artificial intelligence . The cybersecurity vendor on Tuesday launched an AI kill switch designed to let security teams stop internal AI agents that go rogue, block them from relaunching and cut off their enterprise network access. The tool is built into CrowdStrike's Falcon Guardian platform, launched in September to secure AI agents. CrowdStrike also announced an integration with Anthropic's Claude Cowork . "Having the ability to control and turn off, and make a decision and decide, I think that's really important for this next chapter of AI adoption," Chief Business Officer Daniel Bernard told CNBC. A string of recent high-profile cyber incidents has added urgency to calls for some kind of emergency shutdown mechanism. The Hugging Face breach orchestrated by rogue OpenAI agents in July was particularly alarming for businesses. Last week, Binance disclosed the largest crypto cyberattack on record and hackers have recently targeted hundreds of refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in France. Over the summer, U.S. representatives introduced bipartisan legislation that would require AI companies to build shutdown capabilities into their models. Critics argue, however, that an emergency stop button is far too complicated to implement across multiple systems, data centers and complex AI models. Read more CNBC tech news Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents OpenAI pares fundraising goal, now seeking up to $20 billion in latest round Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion hack, says 90% of stolen user assets are covered Why AI is boosting Meta’s ad business while hurting Google search Bernard said the kill switch operates like a light switch in systems where customers use its Falcon platform. The process can detect internal agent activity but requires a human to decide whether it's benign or malicious, he added. "If you kill a process at the root, and we have that level of access at the root … it's very binary," Bernard said. "You either kill the AI and the agent, or you don't, and then you report on that." In the age of AI, businesses are moving quickly to adopt autonomous tools, often without the necessary safeguards and protections. CrowdStrike believes its new tool will let companies stop AI agent 'misbehavior in its tracks, while leaving room for innovation. The company also announced plans to acquire AI observability startup Fiddler AI and AI security testing firm Dreadnode . CrowdStrike and its rivals are rapidly scooping up cybersecurity startups to keep up with increasing security demands. headlines.article_text: Pfizer (PFE) earnings Q3 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Pfizer reported third-quarter results that topped estimates and hiked its full-year outlook, citing its "strong year-to-date performance" and ongoing cost cuts. Pfizer also announced that Cecile Guegan, who has held various finance leadership roles at the company over the last two decades, stepped in as chief financial officer this month. In this article PFE Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:18 04:18 Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla on Q3 earnings, patent expirations, obesity drug market The Exchange Pfizer on Tuesday reported fiscal third-quarter results that topped estimates and hiked its full-year outlook, as demand for its newly launched and acquired products grows. Pfizer also Tuesday announced that Cecile Guegan , who has held various finance leadership roles at the company over the last two decades, stepped in as chief financial officer this month. She had served as interim CFO since August, when Pfizer's former CFO, Dave Denton, stepped down to take the same position at Nike. The company is now expecting full-year revenue to total $62 billion to $64 billion, which compares with a previous outlook of $60.5 billion to $62.5 billion. The low end of that sales range would be roughly flat or down slightly compared with 2025 revenue of $62.6 billion. Still, Pfizer cited its "strong year-to-date performance" as a driver for the guidance hike. In an exclusive interview with CNBC, Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla said the company's Covid product revenue was "very low" this quarter and year, but called it "positive news for us." "Covid revenues was an overhang on the performance of our stock because of the perception that it is volatile and it's material to us. Actually, we've proven that we can make it irrelevant," Bourla said. "If anything, only an upside because, in the lowest possible Covid performance, we are beating, and we are raising by $1.5 billion because of the overperformance of the other products." Pfizer reaffirmed its Covid product outlook of roughly $4 billion for the year, expecting the majority of Covid shot sales in the fourth quarter during vaccination season, Guegan said during the call. The pharmaceutical giant now expects full-year adjusted profit of between $2.95 and $3.05 per share. That compares with previous guidance of between $2.80 and $3 per share. Smith Collection | Archive Photos | Getty Images That includes a one-time $650 million charge, or a negative impact of 10 cents per share, recorded in the third quarter tied to the company's licensing and collaboration agreement with Chinese cancer drugmaker Innovent Biologics. Pfizer is working on a comeback story after its massive pandemic-era success waned. As demand for Covid products drops and generic rivals threaten its biggest moneymakers, Bourla is looking to jump-start growth through strategic acquisitions, fresh cancer drugs and a big bet on weight loss treatments through its acquisition of Metsera. "In addition to the revenues that they generate now, and they will continue generating so that we can overcome the patent, the loss of patent exclusivity, we are bringing pipeline that will perform even better in terms of growth," Bourla told CNBC, referring to Pfizer's launched and acquired products. Pfizer in August expanded its multiyear cost-cutting efforts to help offset sharp declines in Covid product sales, and is now targeting roughly $9.7 billion in net savings through 2029. Here's what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 87 cents adjusted vs. 73 cents expected Revenue: $16.58 billion vs. $15.87 billion expected Pfizer reported third-quarter revenue of $16.58 billion, relatively flat from the same period a year ago. The company cited an operational decrease of $57 million, primarily due to lower Covid revenues, and a $15 million negative impact from foreign exchange. That was offset by strong sales of key products like its blood thinner Eliquis and targeted cancer drug Padcev, which jumped and beat expectations. Eliquis in particular raked in $2.52 billion in sales, up 25%. Analysts were expecting revenue of $2.40 billion, according to StreetAccount. Padcev posted $720 million in revenue for the period, which compares with the $658 million that analysts were expecting. Sales of Pfizer's newly launched and acquired products contributed $3.8 billion, growing 32% operationally, Guegan said during the earnings call. That includes Padcev, its respiratory syncytial virus vaccine Abrysvo, its pneumococcal shot Prevnar 20 and oral lung cancer drug Lorbrena, among several other products. 'We continue to invest behind this group of products to mitigate [loss of exclusivity] headwinds over the next several years," Guegan said. "In addition, this quarter's performance demonstrates clear progress against our objective of returning to growth toward the end of the decade." Pfizer's Covid products also topped estimates for the quarter despite seeing steep sales declines. The company's Covid vaccine generated $808 million in sales, which compares with the $770.4 million that analysts were expecting, StreetAccount estimates show. Meanwhile, Pfizer's antiviral pill, Paxlovid, booked $449 million in sales, coming in above the $394.1 million that analysts were expecting. The company booked net income of $3.24 billion, or 56 cents per share, for the period. That compares with net income of $3.54 billion, or 62 cents per share, during the third quarter of 2025. Excluding certain items, including restructuring charges and costs associated with intangible assets, Pfizer posted earnings per share of 87 cents for the quarter. headlines.summary: Ken Chenault, who served 17 years as American Express CEO, says some political situations call for a firm stance from business leaders.

Icon Sportswire | Icon Sportswire | Getty Images When a CEO talks politics, people tend to get nervous — especially when the issues don't seem to directly affect the company. Yet "some fundamental issues" call for a public stance, even if the subject doesn't obviously or immediately affect a CEO's company, former American Express CEO Ken Chenault told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday. Any threat to democratic institutions or processes in the U.S. can ultimately sow political and economic instability that could have a negative impact on any business, regardless of the sector or industry, he added. "If you want to build an enduring company, you should care about what happens in our society," said Chenault, who stepped down as American Express CEO in 2018 after 37 years at the financial services giant, including nearly 17 as chief executive. He currently serves as chairman and managing director of venture capital firm General Catalyst. CEOs shouldn't speak out on every political matter, Chenault said. But those seeking lasting success need "long-term perspective" about any risks and opportunities that could ultimately affect their companies, he suggested. Business leaders often refrain from speaking out on political issues for fear of alienating customers or their own employees . Some companies have found success weaving politics into their public image — outdoor apparel company Patagonia is among the best known — but taking a publicly political stance is most often met with mixed opinions, according to a 2025 study from a group of Ivy League researchers. On the whole, the average person generally prefers CEOs to stay silent on divisive political issues, the study found. Yet with American voters heading to the polls on Tuesday, Chenault specifically pointed to the issue of voting rights as one that corporate leaders like himself should publicly acknowledge. As the Republican Party braces to potentially lose national and state-level seats in the midterm elections , President Donald Trump has declined to say he would unconditionally accept the electoral results. Instead, the president has promised to accept the results "if they're honest elections," The Washington Post reported on Oct. 27. "If, in fact, the upcoming election is threatened and the verdict of the election is not accepted, that is not an issue that I would be quiet [on]," Chenault said, adding: "Nothing is more fundamental than preserving and strengthening our democracy [and] the fundamental right to vote." Political instability can hurt a country's economy, research suggests . One potential path for democratic erosion to harm business: A breakdown of the rule of law can scare off investors looking to deploy capital or build new companies, Princeton University political scientist Layna Mosley found in a July 2023 report published by nonpartisan organizations The Brookings Institution and States United Democracy Center. As American Express CEO, Chenault weighed in publicly on some political issues that did have an immediate impact on his company. One of his more prominent stances was an acknowledgment of the financial industry's need to adapt and accept additional regulatory oversight following the 2008 financial crisis, for example. More recently, Chenault has spoken somewhat frequently about the importance of robust voting rights. In March 2021, he and former Merck CEO Ken Frazier called on corporate leaders to push back on political efforts to restrict voting access in the U.S. In particular, Chenault — one of the first few Black CEOs of a Fortune 500 company, upon his appointment at American Express in 2001 — spoke out against policies that voting rights groups have criticized as disproportionately disenfranchising voters of color. "Corporations have to stand up. There is no middle ground," Chenault told "Squawk Box" on March 31, 2021. "This is about all Americans having the right to vote, but we need to recognize the special history of the denial of the right to vote for Black Americans, and we will not be silent." Minh Connors | Bloomberg | Getty Images Meta is seeking to raise between $20 billion and $25 billion in a bond sale on Tuesday as the company ramps up its spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure along with AI models and services. The debt sale is expected to be two-thirds in U.S. dollars and one-third in euros, according to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be named because the details are private. Final pricing for the bond sale should come Tuesday afternoon, the sources said. Meta declined to comment. Bloomberg News first reported on Meta's plans. Meta's bond sale comes days after S&P Global Ratings revised the company's outlook from AA- stable to AA- negative, citing "uncertainty" about its hefty capex spending and negative free cash flow. In its third-quarter earnings report last month, the Facebook parent revealed that its full-year capex will come in between $135 billion to $145 billion, representing a $5 billion increase to the low end of its previous guidance. Meta posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion for its latest quarter, joining Alphabet and Amazon in reporting a negative figure. Meta previously raised $25 billion in an April bond sale, and said last week that it plans to raise $95 billion in an effort to fund its AI initiatives. Of that, Meta intends to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, and an additional $60 billion through an at-the-market program. Meta's stock rose 2.7% on Tuesday after dropping in 12 of the prior 14 trading sessions and closing out October with its worst month in four years. headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: AAPL, PLTR, NVDA, COIN, BE Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. Coinbase — The cryptocurrency exchange's stock rallied 8% Tuesday after sliding 15% in the three trading days through Monday. Coinbase reported third-quarter results postmarket last Thursday showing weaker crypto trading volumes, leading Morgan Stanley to lower its rating to underweight and slash its price target by 53% Monday. Shopify — The e-commerce platform's stock fell more than 5% Tuesday after the company missed estimates on subscription gross profit and gross merchandise volume. Overall, quarterly revenue came in at $3.74 billion, just below LSEG estimates of $3.75 billion. Shopify said it sees revenue growth in the "low thirties" range year over year for the fourth quarter, versus LSEG estimates of 32.1%. Shopify expects free cash flow margin to be consistent with the fourth quarter of 2025 . Bloom Energy — The maker of solid oxide fuel cells saw shares gain nearly 10% after Barclays upgraded Bloom to overweight from equal weight on Tuesday. The bank cited higher-than-expected demand, but lowered its 12-month price target to $289 from $319, which still implies upside of about 47% from Monday's close. Thomson Reuters — Shares slipped 7.5% after Thomson reported weaker-than-expected earnings. In the third quarter, the content and technology provider delivered adjusted earnings of 81 cents compared with 83 cents that analysts polled by FactSet had estimated. Revenue was in line with estimates at $1.83 billion. ON Semiconductor — Shares advanced 4% after ON posted third-quarter results that topped estimates. Adjusted earnings for the period totaled 90 cents per share on revenue of $1.72 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG estimated 88 cents a share on $1.70 billion. DuPont de Nemours — Shares climbed about 9% after the giant chemical company reported third-quarter financial results . DuPont posted adjusted earnings of $2.09 on revenue of $1.87 billion, versus the FactSet consensus estimate of $1.87 per share on $1.84 billion. DuPont raised the full-year financial outlook and expects organic growth to be about 4.5%. Fiserv — The financial services and fintech company's stock gained 12% after third-quarter earnings surpassed estimates. Fiserv earned an adjusted $1.75 per share against the FactSet consensus estimate of $1.72. Fiserv also expects to repurchase $500 million of common stock in the fourth quarter under its existing buyback authorization. Artificial intelligence plays — A slate of stocks tied to the AI trade perked up after several days of hard selling. The iShares AI Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) jumped 2%, while shares of chipmakers Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices bounced 3% and 5%, respectively. Shares of memory stock Sandisk advanced almost 4%, and shares of neocloud names Nebius and Ire gained 7% and 9%, respectively. Revvity — Shares gained 11% after the life sciences company raised full-year pro forma adjusted earnings per share guidance to $5.40 to $5.45 from a previous range of $5.30 to $5.40. Pfizer — The pharma giant's stock eased 1% after reporting third-quarter results. Pfizer earned 87 cents per share, excluding one-time items, on revenue of $16.58 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG estimated a profit of 73 cents per share on revenue of $15.87 billion. Zebra Technologies — The maker of barcode scanners and mobile computers used in retail and other industries saw shares fall 6% after third-quarter adjusted gross margin came in at 46%. The FactSet consensus estimate was for 47.7%. Top- and bottom-line results for the period beat expectations. Gartner — Shares slid 13% despite third-quarter results beating expectations. Gartner also issued better-than-expected adjusted earnings and revenue guidance for the full year. Palantir Technologies — Palantir shares fell 2% despite the company's third-quarter adjusted earnings topping Wall Street's estimates. The company's U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, topping U.S. government revenue of $953 million. Palantir also projected about $2.65 billion in fourth-quarter revenue and $8.53 billion for all of 2026. Apple — Apple shares weakened 2% after the iPhone maker reported a disappointing margin forecast , and as iPad sales in the fiscal fourth quarter missed the Street's estimates. — CNBC's Deena Zaidi, Scott Schnipper, Davis Giangiulio, Darla Mercado and Fred Imbert contributed reporting.
